newsitem.title: UK: Plants may use chemicals to help one another.
newsitem.headline: Plants may use chemicals to help one another.

text.p: Plants may be able to send out chemical signals that help one another resist invaders such as viruses, scientists reported on Wednesday.
A group working at Rutgers University in New Jersey found that infected tobacco plants send out a gas that seems to help neighbouring, uninfected plants resist the tobacco mosaic virus.
Ilya Raskin and colleagues were concentrating on salicylic acid, more commonly known as the active ingredient in aspirin, to see whether it was involved in virus resistance.
Tobacco plants inoculated with the virus produced a gas version of methyl salicylate, also known as oil of wintergreen.
To see if it acted as a signal, they grew plants in airtight chambers that had airways connecting them. They inoculated some plants and put normal healthy plants in the adjacent chambers.
The neighbouring plants also became resistant to the virus, even though they had not been inoculated, the scientists reported in the science journal Nature.

"This demonstrates the possibility that plants attacked by disease-causing pathogens can signal to neighbouring plants, alerting them that they are in danger of getting sick and warning them to turn on their defences," Raskin said.
"It may also illustrate the way a plant might communicate between its healthy and sick parts."
Plants are known to signal to one another. Acacias being browsed by elephants or giraffes produce ethylene gas to warn their neighbours to produce distasteful poisons that send grazers elsewhere.
But Raskin said this was the first instance of a sick plant signalling in a way that can confer resistance.
"To our knowledge, methyl salicylic acid is the first airborne signal to be shown to be involved in communication between infected and healthy plants," Raskin's group wrote.
They said they did not know if the signal worked in the wild, but it might build up in dense foliage.
Other biologists welcomed the report. "This is an exciting discovery," said Clarence Ryan of the Institute of Biological Sciences at Washington State University.
"The question of how plants communicate insect and pathogen attacks to alert the defensive responses of nearby plants has been raised for decades by ecologists."
